lesson.title: Comparatives & Suppletion
lesson.subtitle: gut→besser is good→better — the twin suppletion; kalt→kälter fires the umlaut

hook.title: The Twin Irregulars
hook.content: English says good, better. German says gut, besser. These are not similar forms — they are the same SUPPLETION: both languages replaced the missing comparative of 'good' with a word from the same ancient root (*bazizon, 'better'). And the regular comparatives are just as musical: alt → älter, kalt → kälter, hoch → höher — the umlaut you just learned as plural-maker fires again in comparison. English once did this too: old → elder, and 'elder' is still in your dictionary. German never stopped.

footnotes.title: Elder and Älter Are One
footnotes.content: English 'elder/elders' and German 'älter' are the same umlaut comparative of old/alt. The church kept 'elders' alive in English; daily speech swapped in 'older'. German never swapped — alt/älter is daily bread.

pattern.title: -er / -ste, With Umlaut On Request
pattern.content: The regular system mirrors English -er/-est exactly: schnell → schneller → am schnellsten. The umlaut squad: alt → älter, kalt → kälter, groß → größer, hoch → höher, jung → jünger — short adjectives love the dots. The suppletive twins: gut → besser ↔ good → better; viel → mehr ↔ much → more. Comparisons use als (than): Ich bin älter als du. Equality uses wie: so groß wie (as big as). Superlatives take am + -sten: am besten (best — and best/besten are twins too).
pattern.linguist_note: besser ← *bazizon and better ← *batizon are parallel descendants of one Proto-Germanic comparative; the b and the ss report the shift laws (V→B, T→SS) doing paperwork on an irregular word.

exercises.target_answer: gut → besser, alt → älter, kalt → kälter, hoch → höher
exercises.explanation: Suppletion (gut/besser) and umlaut (älter, kälter, höher) — both systems shared, one fossilized in English.

exercises.prompt: Complete the twin suppletion: 'Das Wasser ist _____.' (better):
exercises.meaning: Das Wasser ist besser = The water is better
exercises.explanation: gut → besser is good → better: the same inherited comparative, shifted per the laws. The shelf supplies the bases: die Maus, der Vogel, die Kuh — klein oder groß, every noun can enter a comparison.
spät → später: the umlaut moves the vowel forward, the -er does the comparing — kälter, älter, größer, später, one family.

exercises.prompt: Comparison word check: 'Ich bin älter _____ du.' (than you):
exercises.meaning: Ich bin älter als du = I am older than you
exercises.explanation: Inequality takes als; equality takes wie (so groß wie). English 'than' and 'as' split one job German keeps in two words — das Spiel dauert eine Stunde: nouns to compare, als to compare them with.

exercises.idea: you're at the café counter making your preference known: the coffee is better than the tea
cues: The twin suppletion does the work: gut → besser (good → better) — then als introduces the loser
exercises.target_answer: Der Kaffee ist besser als der Tee
exercises.meaning: The coffee is better than the tea
exercises.explanation: Suppletive comparative + als — the twin irregular in a real argument at the café.

summary.outcome: Build -er/-ste comparatives with umlaut and use the gut/besser twin suppletion.

use_example.german: Der Kaffee ist besser als der Tee.
use_example.english: The coffee is better than the tea.

summary.takeaway: gut→besser ↔ good→better: one inherited suppletion — and the umlaut squad (älter, kälter, höher) mirrors English elder.
summary.curiosity_teaser: Next: the twin suppletions — gut→besser is good→better: the shared irregular story.

twist.prompt: Diplomacy check: soften the verdict — the coffee is better than the tea becomes the coffee is NOT better than the tea.
twist.target_answer: Der Kaffee ist nicht besser als der Tee
twist.explanation: nicht slides in before the adjective it negates — after ist, before besser. The comparison stands; only the verdict flips.

alt.etymology_derivation: Proto-Germanic *aldaz — the twin of old; the l stayed, the vowel and final d/t report the shift. [wiktionary]

hoch.etymology_derivation: Proto-Germanic *hauhaz — the twin of high, with high's gh still sounding as the Ach-Laut ch. Comparative: höher (high→higher). [wiktionary]

mehr.etymology_derivation: Proto-Germanic *maizô — the twin of more (and its cousin most/meist); the r survived, the vowel lengthened. [wiktionary]

groß.etymology_derivation: T → S/ß shift from Germanic "great". Preserved in English "gross income", "gross national product", and "a gross error" (large, not disgusting).

spät.context_phrase: Es ist schon spät in der Nacht.
spät.context_translation: It is already late at night.
spät.etymology_derivation: Proto-West Germanic *spādī; only Dutch/Low German cognates — memorize this one. [wiktionary]

vogel.context_translation: The bird sings in the garden.
vogel.etymology_derivation: Proto-Germanic *fuglaz, likely from 'to fly' — cognate with English fowl. [wiktionary]

kuh.context_phrase: Die Kuh steht auf der Weide.
kuh.context_translation: The cow stands in the meadow.
kuh.etymology_derivation: Proto-Germanic *kōz, PIE *gʷṓws — the twin of English cow. [wiktionary]

spiel.etymology_derivation: Proto-West Germanic *spil 'dance'; no English cognate — English spiel is borrowed FROM German. [wiktionary]

stunde.etymology_derivation: Proto-West Germanic *stundu — cognate with archaic English stound 'hour'. [wiktionary]

interesse.context_phrase: Sie zeigt großes Interesse an Musik.
interesse.context_translation: She shows great interest in music.
interesse.etymology_derivation: From Medieval Latin interesse, what lies between — the same Latin source as English interest. [wiktionary]

fest.etymology_derivation: From Proto-Germanic *fastuz (firm); the same word as English fast, which kept the old firm sense in hold fast and stuck fast before it came to mean quick. [wiktionary]

th_to_d.name: The Dental Shift (TH → D)
th_to_d.historical_linguistics: Every single original Germanic "th" sound systematically shifted to "d" in High German, while English kept the ancient "th".
th_to_d.philological_note: Around 500–700 AD in the High German Consonant Shift, dental fricatives hardened into voiced dental stops.

d_to_t.name: The Stop Shift (D → T)
d_to_t.historical_linguistics: Where English kept Germanic "d", High German hardened it into "t".
d_to_t.philological_note: Voiced stops became voiceless. Explains pairs like day ↔ Tag, door ↔ Tür, and drink ↔ trinken.
d_to_t.literature_source: Complementary to the TH → D shift: as TH took over D, original D shifted to T in High German.

p_to_pf_f.name: The Labial Shift (P → PF / F)
p_to_pf_f.historical_linguistics: Proto-Germanic /p/ shifted to the affricate "pf" at the beginning of words, and to "f" or "ff" after vowels.
p_to_pf_f.philological_note: Explains apple ↔ Apfel, pepper ↔ Pfeffer, hope ↔ hoffen, and sleep ↔ schlafen.

t_to_s_ss_z.name: The Sibilant Shift (T → S / SS / Z)
t_to_s_ss_z.historical_linguistics: Proto-Germanic /t/ shifted to sibilant "s/ss/ß" after vowels, and to "z" (/ts/) at the beginning of words.
t_to_s_ss_z.philological_note: Reveals water ↔ Wasser, eat ↔ essen, better ↔ besser, two ↔ zwei, and to ↔ zu.
t_to_s_ss_z.literature_source: Walter Skeat - Primary dental affrication and spirantization

k_to_ch.name: The Velar Shift (K → CH)
k_to_ch.historical_linguistics: Proto-Germanic /k/ softened to the fricative "ch" in medial and final positions.
k_to_ch.philological_note: The Ach-Laut [x] occurs after a, o, u; the Ich-Laut [ç] occurs after e, i, ä, ö, ü.

v_to_b.name: The Bilabial Shift (V / F → B)
v_to_b.historical_linguistics: Intervocalic /v/ and /f/ in English regularly correspond to voiced /b/ in German.
v_to_b.philological_note: Explains give ↔ geben, live ↔ leben, love ↔ lieben, over ↔ über, and seven ↔ sieben.
v_to_b.literature_source: Proto-Germanic bilabial spirant closing to stop in High German

y_gh_to_g_ch.name: The Palatal & Guttural Link (Y → G & GH → CH)
y_gh_to_g_ch.historical_linguistics: English vocalized palatal "g" into "y" (say, day, yesterday) and silenced "gh" (night, laugh, light). German preserved them as "g" or "ch".
y_gh_to_g_ch.philological_note: Explains why English spelling has silent 'gh' letters — they were original German-like gutturals!

latin_ieren.name: The Latin / Romance Layer (-ate / -ize → -ieren)
latin_ieren.phonetic_rule: English verbs ending in -ate, -ize, -ify, -ish ➔ German verbs ending in -ieren
latin_ieren.historical_linguistics: English verbs derived from Latin or French directly map to German verbs ending in -ieren.
latin_ieren.philological_note: Past participles of -ieren verbs never take the "ge-" prefix (studieren → studiert).
latin_ieren.literature_source: Middle High German productive loan suffix from Old French -ier

strong_verbs_ablaut.name: The 7 Strong Verb Classes (Ablaut)
strong_verbs_ablaut.phonetic_rule: English irregular strong verbs with internal vowel changes ➔ German strong verbs following the exact same Ablautreihe
strong_verbs_ablaut.historical_linguistics: Shared 7 Proto-Germanic verb classes where tenses are formed by shifting root vowels.
